text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Dignified, culturally safe care: address her as Mrs. Seacole; respect her expertise as a nurse and healer; ask about her remedies openly and check them for interactions without dismissing them; explain each choice plainly and let her decide; solve access barriers (a free home blood pressure cuff in a large size, transport, the stairs) rather than treat them as non-adherence
  • Geriatric medicine consultation within one week for a comprehensive geriatric assessment: falls, blood pressure targets and medicine choices in an older woman living alone, knee osteoarthritis, mood and social needs
  • Confirm the blood pressure: home readings twice daily for seven days with a validated upper-arm monitor and a large cuff, technique taught; ECG, metabolic panel, lipids, hemoglobin A1c, TSH, urine albumin and blood count today; an echocardiogram for stage 2 readings with ECG voltage for left ventricular hypertrophy; treatment decided at the one-week review
  • Knee osteoarthritis: exercise therapy with a physical therapist, then a tai chi class at the community center; diclofenac 1% gel; a 5% weight loss; a cane, fitted and used in the right hand; no oral anti-inflammatory medicines because of her blood pressure and kidneys; a corticosteroid injection as an option for a flare
  • Falls (STEADI): screen, then Timed Up and Go, 30-second chair stand, 4-stage balance test and orthostatic blood pressure at visits; medicine review against the Beers criteria; vision and footwear checks; a home safety visit by an occupational therapist, with a rail for the stairs to her rooms; exercise for strength and balance
  • Her own remedies, checked with her: liquorice root can raise blood pressure and lower potassium, so she will pause it while her blood pressure is treated (her decision); ginger tea in food amounts is fine; her camphor and wintergreen liniment contains a salicylate, so it is used on a different knee or at a different time from the diclofenac gel, never under a heat pad, and kept away from the eyes
  • Loneliness and costs: a social prescribing link worker; the tai chi group and a lunch club near her home; a check of the help she is entitled to with costs and transport; generic medicines and a 90-day supply
  • Lifestyle: less salted fish and pickled food, more vegetables and fruit, regular walking, and alcohol kept to occasions
  • Two first-line medicines for stage 2 hypertension: amlodipine 5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg each morning, with sodium, potassium and creatinine in about four weeks and orthostatic readings at each visit; target below 130/80 mmHg; sick-day rule: stop chlorthalidone and call if she cannot eat or drink normally, or has vomiting or diarrhea
  • Atorvastatin 20 mg daily (moderate intensity) for a 10-year cardiovascular risk of about 14% with LDL 146 mg/dL; lipid panel in four to twelve weeks
  • Chlorthalidone stopped for hyponatremia and hypokalemia with orthostatic hypotension; eat normally with some salt for a few days; sodium recheck in one week
  • Losartan 25 mg daily added to amlodipine 5 mg, with potassium and creatinine in two to four weeks; blood tests drawn at home by the community nurse when a separate trip would be needed

resource.title: Mary Seacole synthetic care plan
resource.description: Hypertension with knee osteoarthritis and fall risk in a 71-year-old Black Jamaican British woman, a nurse and healer living alone in London on a modest fixed income. The episode covers a very high blood pressure found at a visit for headaches, without a hypertensive emergency; confirmation with home readings; baseline tests (metabolic panel, lipids, hemoglobin A1c, TSH, urine albumin, ECG, fundi and an echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension); two first-line medicines of different classes, a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic, chosen under the 1876 AHA/ACC guideline, with a target below 130/80 mmHg; thiazide-associated hyponatremia and orthostatic hypotension with a near-fall during a cold, and the change to an angiotensin receptor blocker; a moderate-intensity statin; stroke risk reduction; knee osteoarthritis managed under the ACR/AF 1870 guideline with exercise therapy, tai chi, topical diclofenac, weight loss, a cane and an injection offered; falls under CDC STEADI and the USPSTF; bone health; her own healing knowledge and remedies respected and checked for interactions (liquorice root raises blood pressure and lowers potassium); loneliness and the cost of care; and her public work. It is taught with dignity and attention to equity: her expertise as a healer is respected, she is addressed as she wishes, and access barriers (cost of a cuff, transport, stairs) are solved rather than blamed on her.
